The `/start/` reading plan is re-voiced as a signed archivist's note from Senior Archivist Sen — same five steps, same computed chapter links, but the guidance now speaks from the desk that canonically reconciles the record, with the lore/codex trust distinction delivered as professional practice rather than site copy. The out-of-world items (Story Engine, Atom feed) sit in an unsigned postscript after Sen's sign-off, keeping the in-world/out-of-world seam clean. Alongside it, a new codex working paper, [Marked Absences](src/codex/marked-absences.md) (Survey Archive working-paper series, author Sen), files the record's known gaps under a five-way taxonomy — sealed (the *Patience First* terminus), unsettled (the two Brother Daires), live (the specimen the record cannot classify), provisional (the Hall of Quiet Instruments attribution), unverifiable (the number of Concordants) — governed by the stated doctrine *mark the absence; do not explain it*. Every entry restates an absence the public record already carries; none adds a fact, names a cause, or links private-thread material. Step 5 of the reading plan points at the paper so a reader never mistakes a gap for an oversight.

- **A reading plan at `/start/`, and the front page's Begin Reading button now points to it** (2026-08-16). Previously the button dropped a first-time reader straight into the full Seasons & Episodes listing with no guidance on where to begin. The new page lays out a five-step path — start with the Tissadelle Shepherd's Arc spine, read a chapter the way it's built (straight through, then the *View from* buttons and scene-by-scene POV lists), keep the reference shelf beside you (with the lore-is-settled / codex-can-be-wrong trust distinction stated plainly), branch out by storyline thread, then go deeper via the Timeline, Codex, Story Engine, and the Atom feed. Every chapter link on the page is computed from the filtered `chapters` collection rather than hardcoded, so a narrowed edition shows only threads it actually carries, a spine-less edition degrades to a pointer at its own listings, and renumbering can't strand the page on a stale id. The Seasons & Episodes intro gained a one-line pointer back to the plan. All copy restates existing published framing (thread registry descriptions, section-index intros) — the page asserts nothing new about the world.

- **Brother Daire enters the timeline at both ends of it** (2026-08-15). Two entries, because the corpus has two Brother Daires and the Archive has never claimed they are one. [1216 AD (1416 UCSD)](src/timeline/1216-life-of-saint-aoife-set-down.md) becomes the **earliest dated event the timeline carries**: the community at Cill Aoife deputises Daire to write down Aoife's life, and he produces the account that survives medieval copying, leaves Earth with the Currach Fleet's founding scriptorium in 2561–2589 UCSD, and is still being read fourteen centuries later against a taxonomy he had no vocabulary for. The entry keeps his method rather than his biography, since that is what the record kept — *mark what is confirmed, mark what is assembled, never blur the two* — and no birth or death date for him survives in any form. [Year -4 (2822 UCSD)](src/timeline/year-minus-4-river-abbey-second-visit.md) fills the modern end of the same spine, and a real gap: the timeline held nothing between Year -11 and Year -3, so Elvira's second visit to the river abbey on the Boyne — where the Fellowship's Brother Daire tells her the sensitivity runs in her mother's line and gives her the word *Overfold*, and where Aldera reads the thinning half a second before Elvira does — existed only inside the two chapters that dramatise it.

  **Neither entry equates the two men**, and the [character page](src/characters/brother-daire.md) now says so in its own section rather than leaving the reader to notice. Four pages link to that page for the abbey keeper while the page itself describes only the scribe of 1216; whether he is the same man, a later namesake in the same tradition, or a title carried by whoever holds the smithy-and-scriptorium role, no record that has surfaced settles. The annotation stating that question in full lives on a `church-space` page, so all three pages state it on their own terms and **do not link to it** — the private-thread link boundary that `validate-content.js` enforces, and which caught the first draft of all three.

- **The Safety Corps gets branches, and the UL triad moves down a level** (2026-08-15). To Dermot's direction: the Corps is divided by **hazard domain** into branches — **Fold Transit Safety** and **AI Safety** named as the two largest — and the inherited Underwriters Laboratories split of research, standards and certification (**Solutions**) no longer describes the top level, surviving instead as subdivisions *inside each branch*. The vocabulary turned out to be already canon rather than new: the command-hierarchy entry has the Academy "organised as a college per corps and a **school per branch**", which the arrangement now explains. The Corps' stated reason puts function beneath domain — *the method is common property and can be taught to anyone; what cannot be taught quickly is the specific way a domain goes wrong.*

  **The AI Safety Branch does not hold the gate**, and the page is careful about it, because canon already assigns commissioning authority over agentic systems to the AI Governance Commission under the Concord Accords. The Branch certifies something narrower and entirely its own: whether a lawfully commissioned mind is fit to be **deployed** where the Rangers propose to deploy it. That is the hull-and-route division the Corps already lives with at a fold gate, applied to minds — *a mind may be lawful and unsuited; the Commission answers the first question and has never claimed the second.*

  **Incident investigation sits outside the branches**, because a branch that certified a hull cannot investigate that hull's failure without becoming its own reviewer. Ordinary investigation reports to the corps president. **A major, cross-disciplinary investigation is led from the command ladder by a Starwarden or above** — which reads at first like a straight contradiction of two existing lines ("none of them answerable to a Starwarden"; "a Starwarden cannot override a Safety Corps finding") and resolves in the word *cross-disciplinary*: a fold-transit loss with casualties is a Safety question about the hull, a Navigation question about the route, a Medical question about what the crew survived, and no corps president holds authority inside another corps. The only office that can convene all of them is on the command ladder. The charter line then holds underneath, unchanged: **command decides what is investigated and does not decide what any corps concludes** — the Starwarden directs the inquiry and cannot amend a single finding brought to it, including a finding that command's own tasking caused the loss.

  **What an investigation produces depends entirely on who is being answered.** Inside the Rangers a finding is not a suggestion: the Corps' standards bind the whole institution, and where an investigation concludes a standard was wrong the Corps amends it and the amended standard binds from the moment it issues, no approval sought. Outside them it produces a recommendation, **referred for review to whichever government actually holds the authority** — the polity that registered the vessel, the habitat administration, the world whose citizens died — which adopts, dilutes, defers or files it as it chooses; where it is declined, the Corps publishes that it was made and declined. *Absolute authority over its own house, none whatsoever over anyone else's* — and the Corps' answer to being asked whether that frustrates it: *a body whose recommendations were binding would be a body worth capturing.*

  **Boundary Safety is named as a third branch and the oldest**, descending directly from the USIS boundary-proximate programme and predating the Star Rangers — which is where the Corps' character was formed, and which finally gives the **certified boundary analyst** designation a branch to live in. **"Solutions" is retired**: the commercial coinage did not survive the body's charter as a public-interest institution, and the arm is called Certification, because *a body whose entire claim is that it has nothing to sell should not name the arm that issues its certificates after a product line.* That leaves the Corps declining two words from opposite directions — *regulator*, which claims a power it does not have, and *Solutions*, which claimed a relationship it did not want. Governance gains a second axis: a **chapter leader** holds a post, a **guild leader** holds a branch, neither outranks the other, and both answer to the corps president — all three held **on secondment from regular duties**, keeping the substantive rank and post and returning to both, which the Corps treats as load-bearing rather than administrative: *the ones who have to live with a standard are the ones who elected the person writing it, and that person has to come back and work to it.* Corps President is confirmed as a guild office and keeps its existing name; **Guild President was descriptive, not a rename**, so no terminology migration is needed. And **a Starwarden convening a major investigation holds nothing outside the Rangers** — where a Ranger appears in someone else's inquiry it is by invitation, as **neutral mediator, arbiter or observer**, a role conferred by the inviting party and revocable by them, *which is exactly why it is worth having*. The [Academy entry](src/lore/star-rangers-academy.md) turned out to corroborate the whole structure independently, being organised as a school per branch precisely because certifying "boundary analysts, ship's pilots, field surgeons, and investigators against a single standard" is "not a hard problem so much as an incoherent one".

  Two further tiers of who is bound, both to Dermot's direction. **Suppliers, subcontractors and their entire supply chain are bound by contract**, on pain of disqualification from future work — a certified assembly containing an uncertified part is not a certified assembly, so the condition flows all the way down, and foundries that will never sell a Ranger hull hold Ranger certification because the yard they sell to must. This is the nearest the institution comes to the power its charter denies it, and the page is precise about the difference: **it binds who the Rangers buy from, not who exists.** A firm that declines has lost a customer, not a licence. **The Dock Seven gap is deliberately left open** — procurement reaches only those who want the business, and the Hyperfold Yield Combine sold to hull operators and wanted nothing from the Rangers. **Donors and supporters are bound by none of it**, holding no certification and asked for nothing but the money; what is examined is whether the money may be taken at all, support being accepted only from legitimate, bona-fide, law-abiding citizens and organisations. That test exists for the same reason the Rangers are self-funding: *a body that can be embarrassed by its donors can be steered by the threat of it.*

- **Three species lore pages, and body plans for the two that already had one** (2026-08-13). The ruling that the Krenyi are the only other sapient humanoids exposed a gap nobody had noticed: **five species had characters on the roster and no described body anywhere in prose**, which is why three of their portraits had quietly drifted humanoid. New pages for the [Veyr Basaltborn](src/lore/veyr-basaltborn.md), [Pelagene Littoral](src/lore/pelagene-littoral.md) and [Serephine Dunekin](src/lore/serephine-dunekin.md); body plans and technological histories added to the existing Chthonari and Verdani entries.

  Each was derived from its world rather than invented, and in several cases the character page had already done the work. Qiren Tal's file had solved high gravity better than any fresh attempt would have — *"a lattice carries compression the way solid bone never could"* — so a **Veyr is a truss, not a mass**, with no fixed front and no privileged pair of arms. Mira of Brine's specialism in *fluid-boundary anomalies* only means something if **Nerath is several fluids lying stably on one another**, which it now is. Sethka Ru's exposure windows turn out not to be a professional discipline but **a metabolism with a career built on top of it**: the Serephine body is closed against a sky that would sterilise it and **unfurls an enormous respiratory surface twice a day**, at dawn and dusk, in the only hours neither extreme kills.

  The set is completed by five distinct relationships with the same bottleneck. **The Veyr were handed fire by their own crust; the Pelagene never had it and never could; the Serephine had to focus it out of the sky; the Chthonari never needed it, because the Undersong Belt is already made of metal; and the Verdani never built the furnace at all**, being limited by light per day rather than by heat. That last one has a consequence worth the whole page: a thallenwort strain is adapted to one biome's light, so **migration is a permanent metabolic cost rather than a decision** — which is the actual reason Verdance has four independent governments instead of one.

- **Portraits for Sethka Ru, Qiren Tal and Isren Farrowkin** (2026-08-13), all three blocked earlier the same day and all three generated first time once the prose existed. Sethka is the closed form caught halfway into the open one at dusk; Qiren is an open lattice with no solid trunk, the bulkhead visible straight through the body; Isren is low and broad with fern-like vanes half-opened to a window and nowhere for a visitor to look.

- **[Sofia Santos](src/characters/sofia-santos.md), and Thalassa's first planet-wide office** (2026-08-13). Drafted to a one-line brief — *charismatic, determined, sharp, green-eyed, the first female president of her planet* — after two collisions with canon were put to Dermot rather than resolved quietly. **No planet in the record has a president** (the only `president` in the corpus is the Star Rangers' *corps president*, a guild office deliberately off the command ladder), and **the setting has no history of women being excluded from power** — eight centuries of Krast, Wender, Shepherd, Drey, Voss, Korvain, an abbess running a first-contact relationship, six generations of women holding the Shepherd croft, and not one page anywhere framing a woman's appointment as a first. Both questions went to him: **Thalassa** for the world, and **first president full stop** for the framing. The office is then built out of what [Thalassa's own page](src/lore/planets/thalassa.md) already said. Two cities that have never agreed how to be a floating settlement can run separate municipal councils for as long as everything in dispute is **above the waterline**; below it there is one ocean, and no council has ever been able to hold half of a tether field. So in 2822 the councils jointly ceded the powers neither could exercise alone — seabed tenure, the mooring-tower tether fields, current loading across shared shoals, the state of the water column — and **nothing else**: no legislature, no revenue, no enforcement, no authority over any person. Dock-priority scheduling, the rivalry SSDC liaison staff call the most reliable source of paperwork on their desk, stays exactly where it was. *Santos holds more jurisdiction than anyone else on Thalassa and cannot schedule a dock.* **The lore page's "no single planetary government" is left literally true rather than amended**, because the instrument's first clause says so itself — that being the only condition on which either city would sign — and everybody calls her President of Thalassa anyway. The brief's charisma is made the mechanism instead of the decoration: an office with nothing to trade can only be exercised by persuasion, so what she has is a room's attention and the load figures, and she has never been the person in the room who understood the figures second best. She is a tether-load engineer, which is why the instrument creating her office is written in vocabulary she had used professionally for a decade. **She declines *first woman* every time**, and not out of modesty — the phrase describes a scarcity Thalassa does not have, both councils having seated women since founding, and accepting it would mean accepting an account of her planet she knows to be false in order to be flattered by it. What she is first at is the office, which she considers the more interesting fact: **she is the first person on Thalassa who can be wrong for everybody at once.** The closing turn is the one the weak office sets up. Two councils built it too feeble to be worth capturing, each expecting the other to try; she has spent four years never once asking for a power the instrument does not give her, through a period when she could have had several for the asking — *which is the part that is not restraint*, since an office that visibly does not reach is the only argument that will ever make either city extend it. She has not claimed otherwise when asked. What she wants is on the record too: the petition for full self-governance Thalassa has never made, which the arithmetic does not yet support, and which nobody has counted more carefully than she has.

- **[Starwarden Luke Valerius](src/characters/luke-valerius.md), who cannot check whether he is neutral** (2026-08-13). Drafted to a one-line brief — *frontier Starwarden in 2826, navigating higher-dimensional anomalies, holding political neutrality among warring human factions, a hard-science pragmatist who privately doubts neutrality is possible near forces that bend reality.* Every clause of it turned out to have a canon answer already waiting, and the page is mostly those answers put next to each other. **Starwarden is exactly this posting**: the rank answers for a fixed post rather than a vessel, and his is boundary-proximate on the outward frontier, monitoring an interface that has held **Class II** — alternating dominance windows, periodic chronometry divergence — for the whole of his command. The brief's *hard-science pragmatist* is not a personal quirk here but **Archive discipline held literally**: he sides with what was observed at the scope it was observed at, treats a claim with no scope as a sentence still waiting for its subject, and will stop a briefing to ask whether a colleague means this membrane, this archecluster or this instrument. Junior officers read it as pedantry for about a year; the Safety Corps reads it as correctly formed and sends him the difficult approaches. The politics is made concrete rather than atmospheric: a boundary interface's **classification governs what may lawfully be done in its approach**, so his readings are worth money to three settlements, two chartered survey companies and a Union-registered salvage combine. **The class is not his** — a classification is a Safety Corps finding and no Starwarden can override one, which is the guild rule rather than a courtesy — so what he holds is everything the finding is assembled from: which readings are filed, in what order, annotated how, and whether an oscillation goes up as a logged event or as noise. *He does not decide the class. He decides what the officers who decide the class are looking at.* Everyone concerned understands the arrangement precisely, which is why nobody has ever asked him for anything. The doubt then comes out sharper than the brief had it, in two halves. **Declining to adjudicate is free at an interface and never free in a room** — two disagreeing readings can be carried indefinitely and the record is better for it, but an unresolved question has a direction, it favours whoever holds the ground while it stays open, and he has never established that the direction his post's open questions run in is one he chose. And the half he has said aloud once, to his assigned mentor, and never written down: **every measurement at a boundary is position-dependent**, his even-handedness is a stance held somewhere, and he has no instrument that would tell him how it reads from anywhere else. He does not conclude that neutrality is impossible, because that claim would need a scope he cannot supply. He concludes that he has no procedure for checking, that the absence of one is not evidence either way, and that both sentences are correctly formed. Then he goes on filing. He carries **more unclassified transients than any comparable post**, which costs him standing with everyone who would prefer a number, and no finding assembled from his readings has been overturned. Drafted with the brief's bare surname and no given name invented; **Luke** supplied by Dermot on reading it, and the page and its slug renamed to match before either had been published anywhere.

- **[Thalassa Vexar](src/characters/thalassa-vexar.md), the best-liked Imperium officer in the Belt** (2026-08-13). Drafted to a one-line brief — *Assistant Deputy Viceroy of the Solar Imperium, sharp, commanding, respected, and known for kindness and fairness* — and placed where canon already had a slot for it: **Assistant Deputy Viceroy is a real post in this world**, the grade [Osric Fenholt](src/characters/osric-fenholt.md) held in the Belt Settlements Directorate, "two full grades below anyone with actual standing to set policy." So she is historical (b. 2551, d. 2619 UCSD), the Imperium having ended in 2609, and her influence has to come from somewhere other than her grade: she is attached to the **Office of the Viceroy** rather than to a settlement cluster, which is the whole career in one line — *the grade was a cluster officer's grade; the desk was outside the Viceroy's door.* The brief's warmth is kept exactly as given and made load-bearing rather than decorative. **Her kindness was the Directorate's most effective instrument**, and she never abused it: delegations that would not speak to the grades above her spoke to her, she never told one of them anything untrue, and everything she was told went upward correctly filed — which is how a punitive administration came to hold the most accurate picture of the Belt it ever had, and to administer the Belt on it. The settlements under her clusters fared no better; the schedules and caps applied as written. What her decency produced was compliance obtained at a lower cost than force. Two beats do the rest. She forwarded **no recommendation in twenty-one years**, because the grade had no line on any Directorate form in which one could be entered; she raised the absence twice in writing, was answered correctly both times, and did not raise it a third. And she was called *Viceroy Vexar* by everyone below her grade and a good many above it, corrected nobody, and — the revealing half — was corrected by nobody senior either, the Directorate finding it useful that the Belt believed it was being dealt with at a level it was not. The closing turn is the one the existing lore had already set up: she staffed the Directorate's seat on the **High Council**, the chamber built to be consulted rather than heeded, and was then retained on the transition staff to help model the Military Space Command's advisory architecture on it — *she had sat in the one chamber of the Imperium in which outer-station representatives had ever been listened to, and she recommended it be built again.* The MSC "inherited both the form and the flaw." She left no memoir and no account of the period after 2609, and the page declines to supply one.

- **[Sildron Drey](src/characters/sildron-drey.md), the MSC's Director of Operations through the Eden years** (2026-08-13). Drafted to a one-line brief — *former MSC Director of Operations, initially supported Krast, later disillusioned* — then given the ending Dermot supplied on reading it: *exhausted, and a nervous breakdown.* She wrote *On the Cost of Speed* in 2698, the qualified staff-paper version of the argument [General Krast](src/characters/maren-solveig-krast.md) would state in one sentence in 2719, and then held from 2711 the one post that had to convert committee findings into tasking orders. So the Eden delays already on the record — eleven months to a committee, fourteen to a preliminary report, six years to follow-up findings — are hers to execute and not hers to decide, and the *Patience First* liability classification carries her signature. **Her disillusionment is not a discovery that the structure was corrupt; it is the discovery that every delay in it was lawful, correct, and defensible in exactly the terms she had supplied.** She gave nine days of technical testimony at the Consolidation Hearing and supplied the figures that became its finding of structural inadequacy without contesting one of them. **Then, the following spring, she took four years of accrued leave and could not do the work when it ended** — *not would not; the distinction mattered to her* — and the MSC, having no line in its medical schedule for what had happened, reached for a classification that let her be paid and kept her name off a duty roster, which its officer corps read the way it read every fitness finding: as something the officer had turned out to be. The page never names the thing and never diagnoses it, per the record's standing habit. It does let the century land: **the successor institutions eventually descending from this one settle that a stress injury is an injury**, the policy 1.21.0 documented the day before this page was written, and nobody writing Drey's file in 2720 was in a position to anticipate it. Her recovery is slow, incomplete, and not a story. **Director of Operations is a new MSC post** and this page is the only thing establishing it, defined narrowly as the staff-side office measured on whether an order was correctly formed rather than on whether it arrived in time — which is what makes the character possible at all. Drafted as *Avalon Hope* and renamed at Dermot's direction; the retired pen name is dropped from the two `story-bible/` provenance notes that carried it, no commit in the reachable history having ever used it.

- **Difenland, Krilzat and Kalenjar — the Kingdom of the Four Islands names three regions** (2026-08-13). Below the island is the region, and the Kingdom names three: **Difenland**, Aduine's upland terrace country above and behind the Abbeylands, whose walls run on the same labour-day rhythm as the Abbey's without the Abbey having anything to do with it; **Krilzat**, Casimor's windward side, uninhabited but for the watch-post and unfarmed, and still the unit in which ordinary speech measures a bad season — *whatever Krilzat lost*; and **Kalenjar**, Ostrel's harbour region, smallest of the three by ground and holding more people than the other two together. **They are not administrative units** — the Common Council's steward answers for a whole island and nothing smaller — but they are how anyone from here says where they are from. Vellamar has none, and the reason is the point: the throne island is divided into court quarters and garden precincts named for what stands in them, because Vellamar was laid out by an administration and the other three were named by people who worked them. The one hook left live for the delegation: *Krilzat* does not sit in the same phonological company as *Vellamar*, *Aduine*, *Ostrel* and *Casimor*, which [la Chapelle](src/characters/emma-la-chapelle.md) has filed at the lowest confidence her register admits and resisted every attempt to write up as a finding. The court's answer, asked directly, was that Krilzat has always been called Krilzat.

- **The Four Islands delegation has names: [Anne de Courtney](src/characters/anne-de-courtney.md), [Ernesto Strozzi](src/characters/ernesto-strozzi.md), [Emma la Chapelle](src/characters/emma-la-chapelle.md)** (2026-08-13). The Xenolinguistics Branch page promised that "the record's translations have error bars, and its translators have names," and then the branch's own flagship case study had none — every delegation reference in the corpus was *a delegation linguist*, *delegation linguists*, *the Corps' own delegation*. Three officers, each defined by what they decline. **Strozzi**, Principal Officer and senior linguist, rendered the Sisterhood's fixed annual render to the Crown as a *tribute* on a cognate that looked secure; it stood nine months at high confidence and went out to three postings inside the Archive's first account of the Kingdom's government, which put the Abbeylands under Aduine's steward in the only record anyone off-world could consult. He keeps the superseded version filed beside the corrected one under his own name, and when the branch asks him to teach it he teaches the mechanism rather than the remorse — *he would have filed it*, and he does not offer the sentence that would soften that. **De Courtney**, Chief Ranger heading the delegation, has forwarded no request for expanded access to the court: not a second site on Aduine, not terrace sampling, not instruments on the caldera rim, none of which the Kingdom has refused because none has been put. She reads every translation before it reaches the Archive — not for the language, but for whether a sentence claims to know something the delegation was not told — and has sent back more of her own people's work than the court has ever refused her. **La Chapelle**, Field Officer, read a common labour term in the Long Accounting as carrying a technical sense the Kingdom's own chronicles no longer hear, filed it at the bottom of her range, and the instruments then looked specifically and confirmed the engineered atmosphere. She refuses the word *discovery* on arithmetic rather than modesty: being right at low confidence is luck, and a branch that only remembers the ones that landed is training its people to file high. **The language is human**, which the pages treat as what makes the work harder — the branch exists for tongues that evolved elsewhere, and here a real cognate did work a real cognate had not earned.

### Changed

- **Three Sorchas, ruled coincidence and said so on all three pages** (2026-08-15). From the same sweep as the fixes below. The record carries three women called Sorcha and the sharpest pair is not the obvious one: [Sorcha Nic Dhiarmada](src/characters/sorcha-nic-dhiarmada.md) is a valley warden on Drithane who **keeps flocks for a living**, and [Sorcha Shepherd](src/characters/sorcha-shepherd.md) is a Tír na nÓg land-registry surveyor whose **surname says so** and whose croft is six generations of Boirinn flockholders — so the coincidence runs a layer below the given name, into the trade. Neither page had mentioned the other, nor had [Sorcha Lichata](src/characters/sorcha.md), the itinerant healer who holds the name unqualified.

  **Dermot's ruling: coincidence**, and each page now carries the note in the pattern [Galen Kane](src/characters/galen-kane.md) already set — *the resemblance is the entire relation*. Nothing joins the Gleann na gCaorach wardenship to the Boirinn Uplands: no descent, no branch of the holding, no contact of any kind. The Lichata note is the one that had to be careful, because her page leaves her origin unestablished **deliberately**, so it states what the coincidence does *and does not* settle — the shared name is not a thread back to either of those worlds, and equally not evidence about where she is from. *A name occurring three times establishes nothing about any of the three.*

- **Fenholt and Vexar were rivals, and the corpus had already said so without noticing** (2026-08-15). To Dermot's ruling: the Directorate's two Assistant Deputy Viceroys were **rival subordinates of the same Deputy Viceroy**. The sweep flagged them for holding the same grade in the same office across the same twenty-one years with neither page aware of the other; what the ruling exposes is that the connection was **already written and load-bearing on both pages**. [Vexar's](src/characters/thalassa-vexar.md) 2594 liaison appointment came from a Deputy Viceroy who noticed her reports *"required almost no reconciliation afterwards"* — and [Fenholt's](src/characters/osric-fenholt.md) were *"routinely resummarized by officers above him."* Those two sentences are opposite sides of one comparison, and nobody had put them together.

  The rivalry is built from that and nothing invented: **he had the figures and she had the room**. He was posted out to the Anchorpoint Cluster and eleven habitats; she was kept at the desk outside the Viceroy's door where the delegations came to her. **It was never a dispute about honesty** — neither ever accused the other of filing anything untrue, and neither had grounds to. It was a dispute about what a report is *for*: he held that one exists to be true and what happens to it afterwards is not the compiler's business; she held that a true report nobody can use has not been filed but stored. Her objection to him is arithmetical — nineteen years of unamended figures and not one Belt condition changed while they were current. His, never stated to her and inferable only from what he did, is that figures reconcile easily when the people supplying them have already worked out what can be heard.

  **Both pages' claims to distinction survive intact, because the two were answering to different clocks.** Vexar's method produced something usable immediately that expired with the Imperium; Fenholt's produced something useless at the time and is the reason anyone can now check hers. The uncomfortable half is hers, and her page already carried it before this: the Reform Movement's successors found their cleanest material in his untouched columns and some of their best in her reports, and had reservations about only one of the two sources. Neither wrote about the other, and **the rivalry survives only in a Deputy Viceroy's own filings**, where the two names alternate according to what the office was about to be asked. His reviewing officers changed several times across those years and her desk never moved once — which is why that office is the only place both names appear together.

- **Thalassa and Voss take the same ruling** (2026-08-15). The remaining two collisions from the sweep, both coincidence, both now stated on each side.

  **Thalassa is a person and a world.** It was the corpus's only character-name/lore-title collision — [Thalassa Vexar](src/characters/thalassa-vexar.md), the Imperium Belt officer, and [Thalassa](src/lore/planets/thalassa.md), the ocean world — and both pages landed on the same day, 2026-08-13, neither mentioning the other. The dates do the work here: **she died in 2619 UCSD, generations before that world's colony charter**, so the note on the world's page can say outright that it is not named for her. *A sea-name on a planet ninety-six percent open water requires no commemoration to explain it.*

  **The two Vosses have a second layer**, which is the reason it was worth stating rather than leaving: [Dagny Voss](src/characters/dagny-voss.md) runs a refinery habitat at Aspenar under a Federation support compact, [Governor Petra Voss](src/characters/petra-voss.md) presides over five habitats in Earth orbit under the Compact, and **both hold orbital posts** — the only other thing the names share. Different polities, no kinship in any record, no dealings with each other.

- **Two further refusals on `what-the-record-refuses.md`** (2026-08-13). **The water world**, refused as a default rather than as a possibility: *undersea* does not mean H₂O, and the danger is not a brief saying water but a brief saying *aquatic* and importing an entire Earth with it — tides, a beach, breathable air above the surface. What a fluid world actually fixes is pressure, density, opacity, thermal behaviour and what will dissolve in it. And **the archetype argument**, which is the objection the cosmology invites: a setting with a Conceptual layer looks like one where *person* might be a template with a shape. **Nothing at any tier of the Cascade specifies a body plan for a mind.** Reaching for a metaphysical reason why minds must be person-shaped is mythification taking the observer's own form and promoting it to a law.

- **`story-bible/species-design.md`** (2026-08-13) — the working ground, including the answer to whether dexterity is required for spacefaring sapience. **Yes; hands no; and it is probably not the bottleneck.** What is required is manipulation finer than the manipulator, and the holding half is the half that gets forgotten — dolphins lack it, elephants have a trunk finer at the tip than a hand and no technology, so a fine manipulator is not sufficient either. High-energy materials processing is the constraint worth using, because unlike manipulation it differs on every world and so generates history rather than anatomy.

### Added

- **`npm test` now fails on byte-identical duplicate images** (2026-08-15). The gate the image pass below wished it had. Nothing in the toolchain could see a duplicate: `checkOrphanImages` asks only whether a file is *referenced*, and both halves of a duplicate pair are, which is why three pairs — six files, three pictures — sat in `src/images/` until a manual `md5sum` sweep went looking. `scripts/validate-content.js` now hashes every image and reports any group of two or more, naming all the paths and the fix.

  **The cost was never the wasted bytes.** A duplicate hides that a page has no image of its own: `frontier-transformation-protocols.jpg` looked like a bespoke illustration and was a second copy of the command-hierarchy photo, so that gap never appeared in any queue. `story-bible/images.md` had recorded two of the three pairs and gone stale on the rest — which is exactly the job to hand to a gate rather than a note.

  **There is deliberately no allowlist**, unlike `KNOWN_UNREFERENCED_IMAGES` next to it, because a duplicate is always avoidable: sharing one picture across two pages takes **one file and two references**, never two files. Where the two pages are in different directories, the route is an explicit `<img src>` in the page body rather than an `image:` field — `lore-entry.njk` hardcodes `/images/lore/`, so `image:` cannot reach across into `hero/`, while a body reference can reach the other way. That asymmetry is the thing to reach for before a second copy ever looks necessary. Verified by injecting a duplicate: exit code 1, both paths named.

### Fixed

- **Alt-text pass: thirty-five rewritten, every one checked against the image** (2026-08-15). Run after the FTL card's stale alt turned up incidentally. Every alt flagged by any of four tests — outdated by an image swap, placeholder language, under 45 characters, or missing — was opened alongside its image and rewritten from what is actually in the frame. **The audit now reports zero short, zero missing and zero absent alts**, and the eleven remaining placeholder-worded alts are correct, because those cards really are placeholders.

  **Eight lore cards were upgraded from plain placeholders to finished designed cards on 2026-08-12 and their alts never followed.** Each still claimed a heading of *ILLUSTRATION PENDING*, a dark blue-black gradient, and that no illustration for the entry existed — all three false of all eight. The cards carry a category header, a line-drawn motif in a soft glow, a title, a subtitle and a strapline, and four of them are amber, sepia or violet rather than blue-black. Rewritten from the images: [Chthonari](src/lore/chthonari.md), [Civilisation Comparison](src/lore/civilisation-comparison.md), [Lagrange Points](src/lore/lagrange-fold-points.md), [Meta-Dimensional Beings](src/lore/meta-dimensional-beings.md), [Military Space Command](src/lore/military-space-command.md), [Mnemari](src/lore/mnemari.md), [Ynys Wydrin](src/lore/planets/ynys-wydrin.md), [Solar Time and Local Calendars](src/lore/solar-time-and-local-calendars.md). **The eleven character cards flagged by the same comparison are correct** and were left alone — those really are *PORTRAIT PENDING* placeholders carrying a name and role, verified against the files.

  **The remaining five are the class the comparison cannot see: alts that were never right.** [year-zero](src/lore/year-zero.md) read *"steampunk gears on a wooden table"* for an embossed metal relief panel with no table in it. **Three different images shared one identical alt** — *"the interior of an empty parliament chamber"* — and none of the three is a view of a chamber: all are tight close-ups of a delegate's electronic voting console with the chamber thrown out of focus behind it. And [formation-of-star-rangers](src/lore/formation-of-star-rangers.md) called a present-day skyline given a sepia treatment *"a vintage view"*.

  **The terse alts turned out to hide four more outright errors, not just thin writing.** [federation-of-sentient-beings](src/lore/federation-of-sentient-beings.md) said *"a cargo spacecraft and earth"* for an uncrewed instrument satellite — no cargo vessel, no crew. [competing-designs](src/lore/worldwrights/competing-designs.md) said *"a sci-fi blue led futuristic tunnel"* for a flat concentric-ring dial with no depth in it at all. And **two pages called the same image a black hole**, which it is not: it is a bright ring of light around a dark disc scattered with specks, closer to a lit dish shot from above. The remaining nineteen were accurate but useless to anyone who cannot see the image — *"a space galaxy background"*, *"an open old book"* — and now say what is in the frame.

  **Two images removed on Dermot's ruling.** The pass surfaced two stock images carrying real-world specifics of the kind this repo has pulled images for before, and he ruled they do not belong. Both are **deleted rather than carded**, following the eight verified stock images of 11 August — a lore page renders cleanly with no image, and absence beats a picture quietly making a claim. `formation-of-star-rangers.jpg` was a **recognisable real city**, One World Trade Center's spire unmistakable under the sepia, standing in for the founding of the corps. `universal-cosmic-stardate.jpg` was an antique dial engraved **in French with a fleur-de-lis border**, on the entry for a count whose whole argument is that it *"commemorates no founding … a spine that honoured an event would belong to whoever owned the event"* — an image that hands the standard to one nation's heraldry. Recorded in `story-bible/images.md` as Batch 3, since neither carries a PENDING card and so neither appears in the placeholder queue. **Worth noting what the July audit did and did not ask**: it inspected `formation-of-star-rangers` and passed it, correctly, on the question it was asking — whether the alt matched the image. Nobody asked whether the image belonged.

  **Three duplicate image assets, deduplicated on Dermot's ruling.** Nothing in the toolchain catches a byte-identical copy — `validate-content.js` only flags images *no* page references — so a full MD5 scan of `src/images/` was run, and it found **one more pair than the pass had**: `hero/glossary-book.jpg` was identical to `lore/canonical-glossary-and-migration-guide.jpg`, alongside the known `frontier-transformation-protocols.jpg` / `star-rangers-command-hierarchy.jpg` and `post-eleven-dimensional-manifold.jpg` / `threnos-omega.jpg`. **The scan now returns no duplicate group at all.**

  The two lore pairs followed `story-bible/images.md`'s own long-standing "Kept by" column rather than a fresh judgement, exactly as that note anticipated (*"which page keeps it is Dermot's call; the other needs a prompt"*) — and **one of the two was then flipped on his ruling**: **Threnos-Ω keeps the ring**, because the same note already calls that file *"the precedent for a membrane portrait"* on that page specifically, so the image had standing there and the old "Kept by" column was pointing the wrong way. [The Common Manifold](src/lore/post-eleven-dimensional-manifold.md) and [Frontier Transformation Protocols](src/lore/frontier-transformation-protocols.md) are the two pages now image-less and recorded as needing one. The Manifold's brief is the harder of the two and the note says why: it has to carry a **shared substrate rather than a boundary**, so a ring or a membrane is precisely the wrong figure for it. The glossary pair resolved differently, because both *uses* are legitimate — a section hero and a lore entry's image — so only the redundant copy went, and `src/glossary/index.md` now points at the lore file. **The direction was forced rather than chosen:** `lore-entry.njk` hardcodes `/images/lore/`, so an `image:` field cannot reach into `hero/`, while an explicit `<img src>` in a page body can reach the other way.

  **That note was also badly stale**, which is worth more than the fix: it listed five duplicate groups, and three had been quietly resolved by earlier work without anyone updating it. The table is now marked RESOLVED with each outcome recorded.

- **Two duplicated page titles, and the Safety Corps' own founding arithmetic** (2026-08-15). Both found by a corpus-wide sweep for date errors and same-name-different-era collisions, run after the Aoife/Daire correction below.

  **`check-related-terms.js` had been warning about two duplicated titles** and nothing had acted on it. *Allocation Units of Cognition (AUC)* and *FTL Mechanics* each existed as both a glossary entry and a lore entry with a byte-identical `title`, and `glossaryUrl` searches the glossary collection before the lore one — so four `related:` terms across the corpus resolved to the glossary stub and the fuller lore page was unreachable by name. The lore titles are now differentiated, which is what the other seven glossary/lore pairs already do (*Archecluster* / *Inside an Archecluster*, *Krenyi* / *Krenyi (Quiet-Built)*, *Plainmark* / *The Plainmark*): [FTL Mechanics: Channels and Their Constraints](src/lore/ftl-mechanics.md) — taking the subtitle already printed on its own title card — and [Allocation Units of Cognition: Cognition as Scarce Infrastructure](src/lore/ai-usage-credits.md), from that page's own opening line. **Retitling the lore side rather than the glossary side is the safe direction**: every one of those four `related:` terms already resolved to the glossary page and still does, so nothing that currently works changes.

  **The Safety Corps page dated itself two ways a century apart.** It says its operational culture *"predates the Star Rangers by nearly seven centuries"* and, twelve lines later, that its mechanism is *"unchanged in seven centuries."* Both can't be seven. The founding anchor is Underwriters Laboratories, **Chicago 1894 CE = 2094 UCSD**; the charter is **2723 UCSD**, so that gap is **629 years — six centuries and change**, while the gap to the present (2626 CE) is 732 and genuinely is seven. The first now reads *more than six centuries*; the second is correct as written and stands.

  **One stale `image_alt` fell out of the retitle.** `ftl-mechanics.jpg` was described as a placeholder *"headed ILLUSTRATION PENDING"* with *"no illustration for this entry"* — the file is in fact a finished title card: PHYSICS in spaced capitals, a line-drawn wave between two circles, FTL MECHANICS under a rule with two subtitles. Rewritten to what the image actually shows. The sweep also found the AUC entry's *"blockchain network"* alt describes circuit traces and falling binary digits, which is loose rather than wrong, and is left alone.

- **The Aoife/Daire gap is fourteen centuries, not six, eight or nine** (2026-08-15). Surfaced by writing the timeline entry above, which cannot state an interval the corpus disagrees with itself about. Twenty-two phrasings across ten files gave the distance from Brother Daire's 1216 AD manuscript to the survey era as **six, eight, or nine centuries**. `UCSD = CE + 200` is arithmetic rather than a conversion table, so 2826 UCSD is 2626 CE and the gap is **1,410 years** — and every stated figure is what you would write standing in the twenty-first century, since eight centuries after 1216 is 2016 and nine is 2116. The canonical glossary's own dating rule decides which end moves (*an inconsistency between two dates is a mistake to fix*), and 1216 is load-bearing everywhere — thirteenth-century, monastic, medieval copying — so the intervals are wrong and not the date. **One figure is not fourteen**: the Currach Fleet's founding scriptorium carried the transcription off Earth in 2561–2589 UCSD, which is 2361–2389 CE, so the Celtic Union picks the devotion up **eleven** centuries after Daire wrote it, not six.

  The sweep reaches [three published S07E01 chapters](src/seasons/s07/e01/s07e01c01.md) including a `canon_facts` line, which is why that half is a separate commit. Nothing in those passages changes but the number: what Aoife met, and whether it held any standing in the Cascade, stays exactly as open as she was careful to leave it. **Two figures were left alone deliberately** — *"remember for a thousand years"* in the lore entry, which is idiom rather than an interval between two dated things, and the Fellowship's *"said Overfold for eight centuries"*, which is a claim about the Fellowship's own vocabulary and not about Daire.

- **Krast's arithmetic: born 2665, dead 2720, and she never saw the Coherence Wars** (2026-08-13). Her page dated the Outer Stations Consolidation Hearing to **2689** and her death to **2714**, against **2719** in the MSC lore, the founding lore, the timeline entry and S00E02C02's `canon_facts` — so the record had her dying five years before delivering the address the page is built around. Chasing that surfaced a larger one the death date had been hiding. S00E02C02 had her say *"I was a junior officer during the last four years of the Coherence Wars"*; the wars ended in **2543**, which put her at roughly **two hundred** in that chamber, against a ~125 cap established the day before in 1.21.0. **No birth year saves the line** — any Krast who fought in the wars is dead a century before the hearing convenes. She is now **born 2665, commissioned 2689** (which makes the chapter's own twice-stated "thirty years of service" exact to the day) and **dead in 2720 at fifty-five**, a few months after the hearing rose. Early for her century; the page says so and declines to say more, because the file doesn't. The war line is reworked rather than cut, and comes back stronger: she now says plainly that she never saw the wars, that nobody in the chamber did, that she was taught them by officers who were taught by the men who ended them — *"and the figures do not change in the handing over."* The figures do not. A judgement handed over with them arrives looking like a figure, which is the thing she had been holding for thirty years without ever having had occasion to check. Nothing in the prose points at it. Two knock-ons swept: her opening no longer has her spending "the rest of her career" on a discovery she did not live to make, and she is now correctly a **witness** at the hearing rather than seated on its panel, which is what the chapter always showed. [Drey's](src/characters/sildron-drey.md) page loses the line making her Krast's junior — under the new dates Drey is three years older and commissioned five years earlier, so the two are contemporaries and not intimates, and Drey's account is that she arrived at the technocratic case herself and would have held it had Krast never existed.

- **The Kingdom of the Four Islands page no longer contradicts itself about how old first contact is** (2026-08-13). Line 30 said Survey Corps contact was "made only in the last several years"; line 80, fifty lines below it in the same file, said diplomatic relations "remain days old rather than years." The *years* reading is the one the rest of the corpus is built on — `what-the-record-refuses.md` twice, `star-rangers-academy.md`'s Xenolinguistics case study, and the story bible — and it is load-bearing, since a **standing pedagogical case study** about failures of patience only exists if the case has run long enough to show a pattern. The outlier clause is rewritten to match: relations are counted in years of translation work and in almost nothing else. Both claims were born in the same 2026-08-10 commit, which landed the page silently inside an image-consolidation PR with no changelog entry, which is how a page came to disagree with itself for three days without anyone reading the two lines together.

## [1.21.0] — 2026-08-13

The release where the setting learned how long its people live, and the record found out it had been describing several institutions it had never named. **Human lifespan is capped at about 125 years**, healthy into the eleventh decade — which sounds like flavour and is in fact the constraint that decides where backstory can be set, because the published seasons and the Founding Era are a hundred and three years apart and no human career reaches across that. It relocated a chapter the same day it was written. The rescue of the orphans who become Karla Wender, Andrew Falkorian and Anne Wender was drafted into the Founding Era, moved to **Year -38 (2788 UCSD)** when the arithmetic made Wender a hundred-and-fourteen-year-old Chief Pilot, and now sits in Season 1's prequel episode beside the Dún Rí chapters. Around it, four institutional facts arrived in one conversation and every one of them turned out to be describing something the corpus already did: the Corps' career structure has **three ladders**, not two; **the Academy stops at Chief** and formal mentoring takes over, which is what Wender had already been doing for Shepherd unassigned since her third year as a Senior; a **stress-related injury is an injury**, which is the policy behind a Season 5 chapter that opens with Shepherd "back on duty" and never explains where she had been; and the **Xenolinguistics Branch** of the Survey Corps had its entire doctrine written across three pages with nowhere to live. Also the first house style guide for the prose, derived by counting the corpus rather than prescribing to it — 175 instances of "does not", 611 em-dashes, and only 26 questions in 70,277 words.

### Added

- **`story-bible/prose-style.md` — the house style, measured rather than asserted** (2026-08-13). Answering "do you have high level guidelines for the style and tone of the narrative prose, using the existing prose as a guide?" by reading the corpus instead of describing it from memory. Every claim that can be counted is counted: **175** instances of "does not"/"did not" across 70,277 words (negation is the primary characterisation tool — people are defined by what they decline), **84** "which is/was" explanatory hinges, **611** em-dashes at roughly one every 115 words, a median paragraph of 12 words against a longest of 120, and **26** questions against 207 dialogue-opening lines, which is why the arguments read as competent rather than probing. The load-bearing finding is that the register is *filed, not narrated* — and that this is what keeps a universe containing cyber-revenants and dead children from tipping into horror. A scene that starts performing its darkness has left the style. Also records the one habit hardest to imitate, in the intake's own words: *"Let a reader find that. Do not let a character point at it."*

- **S01E00C04, *A Person's Name*** (2026-08-13) — three machines reach a ship that no longer answers, and within minutes of the carrying, one of the children makes a name only she will ever use. Three POV blocks: Anne on the ninth day of the wreck, Andrew four decks down in Xenon's bay, Anne arriving at Eden. The lost machines are never stated — Anne counts eight small service units out through the door port and five back, and "gave the two numbers to nobody" — and Andrew, asking Xenon what the empty cradles are for, gets *"They are the right size for the machines that go out first"* and then does not ask the next question, because "some instinct that had grown in him over nine days told him which questions had floors under them." Karla's naming of Lucene-9000 is deliberate rather than a slip: a pause first, and watching the machine's face "the way you watch a door you are deciding to walk through." Anne hears her own name inside *Lucy Anne*, notices it "the way you notice a draught: once, completely, and without the first idea of what to do about it," and calls her Lucene for the rest of her life without ever saying why.

- **Character pages for [Andrew Falkorian](src/characters/andrew-falkorian.md), [Xenon](src/characters/xenon.md) and [Lumbarian](src/characters/lumbarian.md)** (2026-08-13). Falkorian's refuses the label he refuses — the page establishes nothing about what he is and states that the record's silence follows his lead, giving him no stereotype-coded traits so both readings stay genuinely live. Xenon's carries the grief three ways and articulates it none: he is not permitted to create new robots, and "maintains the ship's machines as if each were the last of its kind. In several cases, this is simply accurate." Lumbarian's renders his standing entirely through behaviour — patted housings, visitors shown him, respected in reports and adored on deck — and never uses the words that would explain it.

- **`src/lore/star-rangers-academy.md` — one academy, a college per corps, a school per branch** (2026-08-13). Proposed as a possible fourth ladder and written as something better: training was *already* guild property (`star-rangers-command-hierarchy.md` had said for months that the command ladder has no input into "guild and training functions"), so the Academy is the largest instance of a rule the repo had already stated and never cashed out. The consequence, in its strongest form: **the Corps' most senior officers cannot change what a certification means.** A High Captain who thinks a boundary-analyst standard is set too high may argue it in front of the Safety Corps faculty like anyone else, and may lose — which is what makes the lower ladder's promise of being *documented, examined and appealable* worth anything, since an appeal heard by the same chain that made the decision is not an appeal. Instruction is a **posting held by serving officers**, never a career track, because a faculty of career instructors promoted by other career instructors would within a generation be certifying field competence it had not recently held; the corps pay for that in syllabus continuity and consider it cheap. **The branch list is open and stated on the page as open** — a branch the record has not described is not thereby absent. Card generated by the committed emblem generator (`rings`, not `shield`: the Safety Corps card is already a shield in a ringed seal, and two shields in one institutional family read as one organisation).

- **The Xenolinguistics Branch, Survey Corps — the first named branch** (2026-08-13). Its doctrine was already complete and homeless, spread across `what-the-record-refuses.md`, `cerebraun.md` and the Four Islands material. The universal translator is refused outright; language is learned, by xenolinguists with AI support, on a division of labour the school exists to enforce — the intelligence aligns corpora and never loses a morpheme, and the linguist decides what a word *means* and **owns the error**, because a kernel-compliant mind will not claim a certainty about meaning it does not hold and hands over candidate readings with confidence stated, "never a voice in your ear pretending to be the alien." Both of its standing case studies were already on the site and are both failures of patience rather than method: the Cerebraun, whose three-part answers were filed as evasion for a decade before anyone admitted that is simply how the species thinks; and the Four Islands delegation, still working a presumed-extinct language under an abbess's slow correction.

- **Formal mentoring above Chief, and Wender as Shepherd's official mentor** (2026-08-13). The Academy stops at the hinge rank because certification is a claim other people can check and command judgement is only ever verified by its consequences, usually too late to instruct. So the mechanism changes: on promotion to Starwarden an officer is paired with a senior officer answerable for the mentorship **as a duty rather than offering it as a kindness** — deliberately, because command wisdom passed along by whoever takes an interest reliably advantages the already well-connected, which is the failure the examined lower ladder exists to prevent. The policy formalises something S05E02C02 had already dramatized: Wender had been reading Shepherd's silences since the woman's third year as a Senior, none of it assigned. The pairing puts both crossings of the hinge rank side by side — Wender came to command from the technical ceiling, Shepherd because rotating through everything left her no other ladder — and the hardest clause is the one that chapter demonstrates: **the mentorship gives a senior officer no standing to ask questions the command relationship would not already justify.** Shepherd's page keeps [Galen Kane](src/characters/galen-kane.md) alongside, and the two are not redundant: one adviser she is required to take seriously, one whose judgement costs her nothing to hear.

- **Leaving and coming back: early retirement, career breaks, extended sabbaticals** (2026-08-13). Negotiated rather than granted, because no schedule written in advance could anticipate what a particular Ranger's service has cost them. **A stress-related injury is an injury** — an institution that certifies competence for a living has never found it coherent to rule a person unfit and then treat the finding as a character judgement. On medical ground the Medical Corps' finding binds command, on the same guild-independence rule that stops a Starwarden revising a boundary standard. Two consequences stated: a record with a gap in it is an ordinary record, and coming back is not resumption — the ones who have done it generally say the first ordinary morning back was harder than anything in the incident that sent them away. This also closes an open question the day's other arithmetic had raised, since Brother Fintan's thirty-one years and departure before pension age is now a documented route rather than an anomaly.

- **The three-stage career structure past active service, and planetary representation as a third ladder** (2026-08-13). Representative standing opens at about **55**; from 55 to about **75** the officer is on the **reserve list** — left active service, not retired, still recallable; full pension is available from **75**, at the Ranger's own choosing. And it is a genuine non-command career path with its own progression — deepening specializations, certifications and decorations in place of promotion — which is what makes a High Captain and a Chief who transfer to the same world start level: not because the standing is honorary, but because the path has its own ladder and rank does not transfer onto it. The reserve stage sharpens a tension `planetary-liaisons-and-recruiters.md` already raised: under 75 she is not a private citizen with a service record, she is **a serving Ranger living at home, on a world the charter forbids the Corps to enter.** Nobody in-universe has made that argument formally.

- **The Krenyi present tense, and the gap that is not a withheld answer** (2026-08-13). The Quiet-Built attend to what is here and what is coming; the past is neither sacred nor suppressed, simply not where they look unless looking returns something usable — and most of what they are known for falls out of that single orientation, including grief that resolves and a state-marker meaning *still relevant here*. The page also names the cost, which they would name themselves: **they are poor keepers of anything whose value has not yet been demonstrated.** Alongside it, a third standing editorial rule in the story bible for a case the existing spoiler rule cannot cover — **some gaps are the answer and never resolve.** The Krenyi origin has no reveal behind it, no chapter discloses it, and no future session should treat the empty entry as a to-do; an unexplained gap reads to any competent drafter as an unfinished job, and that instinct is the failure mode. The test for spotting another one: if a page argues for *why* a gap exists, the gap is load-bearing.

- **Galahad Thorne left a difficult marriage before the Threshold posting** (2026-08-13). Written to the cast principles rather than around them: **there is no version of the account in which someone was a villain**, and he does not offer one. The twelve years were long frontier missions — six stations, years at a time — and a marriage conducted across that distance is a thing two people either build deliberately or lose by degrees while both of them are being reasonable. He does not describe her at all, which, given how precisely he describes everything else, is the most deliberate silence on his record. He treats it as neither a wound nor a lesson, which are the two things people usually make of a marriage that ended; he treats it as something that happened and finished. The page names the tempting inference and refuses it — that this is what made him ready for Elvira. He was not made ready by it. He arrived at the Marsh Causeway as a man who had already found out, once, what it costs to be away.

- **Asteria mentored Karla Wender, and the dates permit exactly one version of it** (2026-08-13). Asked with the condition attached — *"if the timelines fit"* — so they were checked rather than assumed. Asteria was already long retired when Galahad Thorne met her on a frontier posting inside his twelve unbroken Survey Corps years, which puts her departure in the early 2820s at the latest, at about a hundred, holding Star Captain. Wender was climbing the certification ladder through precisely that period: a Novice around the turn of the century, a Chief by the early 2820s, and not a Starwarden until after Season 1 opens. **The two careers overlap for the whole of Wender's ascent and not for a day of her command** — so Asteria was never her assigned mentor, because the formal pairing begins at Starwarden and by then Asteria was on a quiet planet running a chapter house. What she gave, she gave to a junior officer on the examined half of the ladder with no policy requiring it and nothing on either record to show for it. That closes a loop the corpus had already half-drawn: Wender now holds the *assigned* version of the duty for Shepherd, and had been discharging it unassigned for years before anyone wrote it down — which is not what the policy asks for and is exactly what she was taught. Asteria's two mentorships now bracket her retirement, one on either side, neither ever an assignment.

- **The Liaison Corps has a name, a second route in, and a ceiling** (2026-08-13). Planetary representation is a **specialist corps** — the Star Ranger Liaison Corps, whose members are **Planetary Representatives** — and its people are serving Rangers on a posting, paid by the Corps, not veterans on an honorarium. The nearest civilian comparison is a police officer moved off dangerous front-line duty and kept on the force, which is also its **second route in**: an injury that does not mend, a condition that will not certify, or a stress injury ends boundary-proximate work for people, and this is where the Corps puts them rather than losing them to a medical finding. Deliberately not a soft landing — the work is needed, hard in its own way, and performed under the officer's own name on a world that judges her by it; treating a liaison posting as somewhere people are put out to is the kind of remark seniors are expected to have grown out of. Being a corps, it elects its own chapter leaders and president, holds its own certification standards, and runs its own Academy college. The entry is retitled from *Retired Rangers: Liaisons, Representatives, and Recruiters* — the word *retired* was wrong in both directions, since they are not retired for the first twenty years and many never retire at all — and the **URL is deliberately unchanged** so that nothing linking there breaks; all nine inbound references are updated to the new name.

- **Corrected: an officer leaving at Star Captain or above cannot join the Liaison Corps** (2026-08-13). Earlier the same day this changelog and two lore pages claimed that "a High Captain and a Chief who take it up on the same world start at the same standing." That is wrong. The corps' senior post is **Chief Liaison Officer** — a Chief's duty title beside Chief Ranger, Chief Pilot, Chief Provost and Chief Science Officer — which places the whole corps on the certification half of the ladder and gives it a real upper bound: **a flag-tier officer is over-ranked for a Chief's berth**, and the Corps declines to invent a grander title to accommodate a large career, because a post inflated for an individual is how a ladder stops meaning anything. So the third path absorbs a great deal of the Corps and is closed at the top of it. Below the bound the original point survives: two Chiefs on the same world start level, and what separates them later was earned in front of that world. [Asteria](src/characters/asteria-the-sage.md) is the worked example of the closed door — she left at Star Captain for a Fellowship of Light chapter house, an institution the Rangers do not run, whose standing rests on having renounced the interests everyone else keeps. Her page needed no change of rank, only the naming of the route she did not take.

- **The maximum retirement age is about 110, and it is the one age nobody negotiates** (2026-08-13). Three ages now bound a career: the Liaison Corps floor at about **55**, a full pension available at about **75** by choice, and a hard stop at about **110** — set where the eleventh decade's borrowed capability runs out, and deliberately *below* the ~125 lifespan ceiling, so a Ranger who serves to the limit still has years in front of her and the Corps simply stops being where she spends them. The stretch between 75 and 110 is the longest optional period in the service and officers use it: Asteria left at about a hundred, a quarter of a century after a full pension first became hers to take.

- **Two more refused tropes: the interfertile alien, and the safe cross-species transfusion** (2026-08-13). `what-the-record-refuses.md` gains a **Bodies and Species** section and two summary-table rows. **No sapient species in this record crosses with another** — no half-human hybrids, no children of two peoples, no breakthrough pending. Not squeamishness: two lineages sharing no common ancestor share no chromosome count, no gene regulation, no developmental sequence, and nothing a gamete could do with another gamete. A trope that treats reproductive compatibility as the default outcome of two people liking each other is not being romantic about biology; it is declining to have any. What the refusal costs is a stock plot and what it buys is better — contact stories that have to find something else for two peoples to make together, of which the Four Islands relationship (years of translation, one standing delegation, nothing else) is already the worked example. The corollary: **cross-species attraction, where it happens, is a fact about a person and not a plot mechanism.** It resolves nothing and bridges nothing, and the universe does not rearrange itself to accommodate it.

- **The Krenyi are demisexual, and their immunity is why the transfusion question has a wrong intuition** (2026-08-13). Attraction arises only through an established bond — the whole species, not a distribution within it — and the page's existing "no flirtation or small talk, straight to material terms" turns out to have been describing that without the word: a Krenyi is not declining to flirt, there is simply no stage of a Krenyi relationship at which flirting would be doing anything. **They do not form romantic attachments to humans and will not consent to interbreed**, stated once and not elaborated, because *why not* asked of a Krenyi is very often the same question as *what are you, really*. Humans do form attachments the other way, and a Krenyi meeting one is generally meeting the mythification problem in its most personal register — a person wanting the Quiet-Built rather than wanting *them*. On the biology, the asymmetry is the part that costs: **Krenyi immunity destroys foreign genetic material outright**, so human DNA entering a Krenyi never persists, which is why "cannot interbreed with any other species" is a flat fact rather than an untested assumption — and running the other way, **Krenyi blood is hazardous to a human**, because transfused antibodies meet a body composed entirely of foreign genetic material and do exactly what they exist to do. The human survives and is seriously unwell for several days at minimum. The clinical file exists because somebody once reasoned, not unreasonably from a species that is honest and rarely sick, that Krenyi blood would do in a shortage.

- **Journal: *The Wrong Century*** (2026-08-13). On putting a chapter a hundred and three years from where it belonged, and being caught not by proofreading but by an unrelated sentence written hours later — the argument for constraints as a machine that checks what you have already written, for free, including the parts you were not thinking about. The entry's spine is the sceptical turn rather than the anecdote: when four further decisions all turned out to be anticipated by existing text, that feeling is *exactly what confirmation bias feels like from the inside*, since a large enough corpus appears to anticipate almost any rule. So it sorts them by whether the earlier writing **predicted** the new rule or merely **permitted** it — a clause that fits a dozen arrangements equally well confirms nothing, while a chapter that opens "back on duty" and never explains where she had been is a hole with exactly one shape. Two predictions and two permissions out of four, and the honest count rather than the flattering one. It closes on **diligence rather than bookkeeping** — bookkeeping being what you do to an account after the fact, diligence a way of working — and on the **harmonic balance between creativity and correctness**, which are not two budgets competing for the same hours: a world too loose to contradict you offers not freedom but the absence of resistance, so nothing pushes back and nothing is discovered, while a world held too tight admits nothing new. In balance, the correctness is not the price of the creativity but the thing that makes it load-bearing.

- **A failed `cpanel-autopull.sh` run now emails `ADMIN_EMAIL` instead of disappearing** (2026-08-13). The question that prompted this was "the photo site autopull should have run at 2am" — and answering it meant reading a deploy email, because nothing else could say whether the run had happened. The run had, and had succeeded; the point is that a *failed* run would have looked exactly the same. `err()` writes to stderr, and cron delivers stderr to the cPanel account's own system mailbox rather than to `ADMIN_EMAIL`, so "nothing to do" and "the pull failed" were both silence. Every deploy outcome was already mailed properly by `cpanel-deploy.sh`; the blind spot was precisely the window before the handoff, the one stretch with no mailer wired up. Exits 1 and 3 now mail directly, with the failure, the checkout's state and the tail of the decision log. **Exit 2 deliberately does not** — on a ten-minute cron a multi-domain deploy routinely outlasts the interval, so a held lock is the expected state, and mailing it would train the alert to be ignored, which is the failure this exists to prevent. No send is ever allowed to change an exit code.

- **`scripts/mail-lib.sh`: the mail transport, extracted so it has exactly one copy** (2026-08-13). The `mail(1)` → `/usr/sbin/sendmail` fallback lived inside `deploy-lib.sh`, which autopull cannot use: sourcing `deploy-lib.sh` runs `mktemp` and `git describe` as import side effects, and autopull sources its libraries on *every* cron run, including the overwhelmingly common one that finds nothing and exits in under a second. So the new file is side-effect-free on source, and that property is load-bearing rather than tidiness. `deploy_lib_notify()` now calls it and keeps its subject format and `MAIL_OK` bookkeeping unchanged. Two copies of a mailer is how one of them silently stops working.

- **`AUTOPULL_MAX_GAP_HOURS` (optional, `deploy.conf`) and a `lastrun` stamp** (2026-08-13). Every run now records that it *fired* — including runs that find nothing and runs that exit on a held lock — because "is cron still firing?" is a different question from "what is deployed?", and only the first can tell you the schedule itself has stopped. `--status` prints both, plus the resolved notification address. Set the new key and a run finding the previous one longer ago than that mails a "runs were missed" alert; unset by default and deliberately so, since the interval lives in cPanel → Cron Jobs and the repo has no basis for guessing one. Its limit is stated in the script, the sample config and the docs rather than left to be discovered: **it can only report a gap on the next run that actually happens.** A cron that stops firing altogether cannot report its own absence, and nothing in this repo can change that.

### Changed

- **Human lifespan is capped at about 125 years, and it is a continuity constraint rather than a flavour note** (2026-08-13). Only the Krenyi, the robots and some aliens are long-lived; medical technology and a fitness culture hold off the quality-of-life effects of ageing into the eleventh decade, so people are not merely alive past a hundred but *capable* past a hundred — a long competence followed by a short decline, and centenarians should not be written with the frailty shorthand a contemporary reader expects. The consequence is arithmetic: the published seasons sit in 2822–2832, the Founding Era in 2712–2723, and **no human can carry a career across both.** A witness to both eras is barely possible at 114, is expensive to write, and has not been used. The story bible carries the check — subtract from 2826, add the age at the time; under about 105 is fine and they can still be working, over 125 is impossible, and between the two the story owes the reader a reason they are still on the page.

- **The rescue moved from the Founding Era to Year -38 (2788 UCSD)** (2026-08-13), drafted and relocated the same day. The Founding Era placement failed on the rule above — a 2717 rescue would have made Karla Wender a hundred-and-fourteen-year-old Chief Pilot — and the replacement year is not arbitrary either: Wender is a small child in the chapter and a Chief Pilot at Season 1's start, having climbed all eight rungs of the piloting track without once rotating off it, and thirty-eight years is what that ladder costs. The chapter now uses Season 1's established prequel convention (`Year -N (YYYY UCSD)`, as in the Dún Rí chapters at Year -4), the `s00/e04/` slot created for the first placement is gone, and the episode index covers both distances. Working ages at the wreck are stated nowhere on the page and are adjustable: Anne about fifteen, Andrew about eleven, Karla about five. The machines are the ones who span real time, which sits comfortably under Lucene's own page and its "continuous service longer than most careers last."

- **`planetary-liaisons-and-recruiters.md` said outright that this was "not a fourth ladder," and it was wrong twice** (2026-08-13).
